analysis.one_liner: Sets national rules for how companies collect, use, and sell personal data, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in November 2023, sent to the Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or any cosponsors before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first nationwide privacy standard for personal data. It would require companies to explain in plain language what data they collect, give people a way to opt out of data collection, require consent before collecting sensitive information like health or precise location data, let people see and delete the data held about them, and ban data practices that discriminate by race, sex, age, disability, or other protected traits. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, and companies over $50 million in revenue would need a designated privacy officer. It never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone whose personal information is collected online — essentially all Americans. People would gain the right to see what data companies hold about them, have it deleted, opt out of collection, and sue-free enforcement through the FTC and state attorneys general. The bill specifically targets discrimination through data, such as ads or prices that vary by race, sex, or disability status.

how_it_helps.text: Companies would have to post a clear, plain-language privacy notice describing what data they collect and who they share it with.

People would gain a right to opt out of having their data collected, and companies would need affirmative consent before collecting sensitive data like health, biometric, genetic, or precise location information.
People could request access to the data a company holds about them, dispute inaccuracies, and have it deleted, and companies could not penalize anyone for exercising those rights.

The bill bans data practices that discriminate based on race, sex, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, religion, age, or disability, including discriminatory targeted advertising and price discrimination.
The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with civil penalties of up to $40,000 per affected individual for violations, adjusted for inflation.
Companies with over $50 million in annual revenue would need a designated privacy protection officer who cannot be fired for doing the job, plus regular internal compliance audits.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting and reselling personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms — would face new compliance costs, limits on what they can collect, and penalties. Some costs could ultimately be passed to consumers through advertising-dependent free services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and big platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill gives individuals no right to sue on their own — only the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce it, which leaves ordinary people dependent on government agencies with limited resources.

The bill allows companies to keep collecting and using data whenever they can claim a 'reasonable interest,' which explicitly includes ordinary marketing practices, so much routine data harvesting would continue.
Companies with fewer than 50,000 individuals' data per year are entirely exempt, and the bill acknowledges compliance costs for small businesses, which would bear some burden relative to their size.

The rules come with broad exemptions for security, fraud prevention, health and safety, and legal compliance, which critics could argue creates loopholes large enough to swallow parts of the standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to individuals are broad and the costs fall mainly on companies that monetize personal data. The design is more modest than the strongest privacy proposals — no private right of action and a 'reasonable interest' carve-out for marketing — so it would blunt the worst data practices rather than end data monetization. But the bill never advanced, so its actual costs and benefits were never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and the 118th Congress ended without any further action.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on November 15, 2023.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No cosponsors signed on at any point.
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and large platforms that profit from collecting and reselling personal data are better off, since no national privacy standard was enacted and their business models remained unchanged. The status quo of a patchwork of state privacy laws also persisted.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DATA Privacy Act and referred it to the Commerce Committee, where it stalled with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral under the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after its referral on November 15, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor took a position, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the bill simply had zero cosponsors [S3].

industries.note: These firms make money collecting, combining, and reselling personal data. The bill would require consent for sensitive data, let people delete their records, and ban discriminatory ad targeting, cutting into their core revenue — and they benefited when the bill died without a vote.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and social media companies
industries.note: Platforms over $50 million in revenue would face mandatory privacy officers, audits, opt-out rights, and data minimization rules that would constrain targeted advertising, their dominant revenue source.

industries.industry: Privacy-enhancing technology and security software firms
industries.note: The bill would fund National Science Foundation research on privacy-enhancing technologies and push all covered entities toward de-identification and anti-tracking tools, creating demand for this industry's products.

industries.industry: Small businesses under the 50,000-person data threshold
industries.note: Entities handling data on fewer than 50,000 individuals per year are fully exempt from the bill's requirements, sparing them compliance costs.
